excerpt: Carrying trips up more Grade 3 children than any other part of addition. Here is the column method explained one carry at a time — including 4-digit sums and adding three numbers — with a quick quiz to check your child.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Open almost any Grade 3 maths notebook and you will spot the same red-pen note more than once: ‘carry the 1!’ Getting 3 digit addition with regrouping right in Grade 3 has very little to do with speed and almost everything to do with one careful habit — lining the columns up straight, then knowing exactly what to do when a column adds to more than nine. This is the written column method only. No mental-maths shortcuts here; just the pencil-and-paper method your child will use in every exam.

I have marked hundreds of these sums, and the mistakes are wonderfully predictable. Once a child understands why we carry — not just that we do — most of those red marks disappear.

What regrouping actually means

Regrouping (older textbooks call it ‘carrying’) is just place value in action. Each column can only hold a single digit, 0 to 9. When the ones column adds up to 14, you cannot write 14 in the ones place. So you regroup: 14 ones is the same as 1 ten and 4 ones. The 4 stays in the ones column and the 1 ten moves next door to the tens column, where it belongs. That is the whole idea. We are not inventing a number from nowhere; we are moving ten of something into the column that counts tens.

Say it out loud with your child the first few times: ‘fourteen is one ten and four ones’. When they can explain the move, they stop dropping carried digits.

Line up the columns before you add anything

The single biggest cause of wrong answers in Grade 3 is not the adding — it is crooked columns. Ones must sit under ones, tens under tens, hundreds under hundreds. Graph paper or a squared notebook helps enormously; one digit per box keeps everything honest.

Always add from the right, starting with the ones column, and work leftwards. Adding left-to-right is the quickest way to end up with a mess of crossings-out, because you often need to go back and adjust a column you thought was finished.

A worked example, one carry at a time

Take 685 + 247. Set it out with 685 on top and 247 below, columns aligned.

  • Ones: 5 + 7 = 12. Write 2 in the ones column, carry 1 to the tens.
  • Tens: 8 + 4 = 12, plus the carried 1 makes 13. Write 3 in the tens column, carry 1 to the hundreds.
  • Hundreds: 6 + 2 = 8, plus the carried 1 makes 9. Write 9.

The answer is 932. Notice that this sum carried twice — once out of the ones and once out of the tens. Carrying more than once in a single sum is exactly what Grade 3 is meant to build, so do not treat it as an advanced extra. It is the main event.

Four-digit sums and carrying into the thousands

Grade 3 numbers reach up to about 9,999, so your child will meet 4-digit sums too. The method does not change one bit — you simply have one more column. Try 1,258 + 1,347: ones give 8 + 7 = 15 (write 5, carry 1); tens give 5 + 4 + 1 = 10 (write 0, carry 1); hundreds give 2 + 3 + 1 = 6; thousands give 1 + 1 = 2. The total is 2,605. A carry can travel all the way from the ones into the thousands, and that is fine — each column just passes its spare ten to the left.

Adding three numbers in one column

Column addition is not limited to two numbers. When you add three, such as 124 + 236 + 118, add every digit in a column, including any carried digit, before moving on. Ones: 4 + 6 + 8 = 18, write 8 and carry 1. Tens: 2 + 3 + 1 + 1 = 7. Hundreds: 1 + 2 + 1 = 4. Answer: 478. The only new skill is adding three small numbers in your head, so keep the numbers gentle at first.

The common mistakes, and the fix

MistakeWhat it looks likeThe fix
Forgetting to carry685 + 247 written as 822Write the small carried 1 above the next column every time
Adding the carry in the wrong placeAdding the carried 1 back into the onesThe carry always joins the column to its left
Crooked columnsTens digit added to onesOne digit per box on squared paper
Writing the whole two-digit totalPutting 12 in the ones columnOnly one digit per column; regroup the rest

Here is the habit I recommend above all others: make your child physically write the carried digit — a tiny 1 tucked above the next column. A carry that lives only in the head is a carry that gets forgotten. On paper, it survives.

faq.q: What does regrouping mean in Grade 3 addition?
faq.a: Regrouping, or carrying, means moving a full ten from one column into the column on its left. When a column adds to more than nine — say 14 ones — you keep the 4 in that column and carry the 1 ten next door, because each column can only hold a single digit.

faq.q: Why do we always add the ones column first?
faq.a: Adding from the right lets each carry move left into the next column as you go. If you start from the left instead, you often have to go back and change a column once a carry arrives, which causes crossings-out and mistakes.

faq.q: Can a Grade 3 addition sum carry more than once?
faq.a: Yes, and it should. A sum like 685 + 247 carries once from the ones and again from the tens. Carrying more than once, and even carrying all the way into the thousands in 4-digit sums, is exactly what Grade 3 column addition is meant to build.

faq.q: What is the most common regrouping mistake?
faq.a: Forgetting to add the carried digit into the next column. The fix is simple: make your child physically write a tiny 1 above the next column every time. A carry kept only in the head is the one that gets dropped.
